name: Last Lantern

stars.name: Last Lantern A
stars.notes: Old, dim K-dwarf primary with very low chromospheric activity and fading luminosity

stars.name: Last Lantern B
stars.notes: Distant red dwarf companion in a wide orbit at 87 AU, posing no disruption to the primary's planetary system

planets.name: Wick
planets.notes: Airless, cratered body in a tight orbit. Surface regolith shows heavy space weathering from billions of years of stellar wind exposure.

planets.name: Tallow
planets.notes: Thin nitrogen atmosphere with trace methane. Surface is a patchwork of ancient impact basins and smooth plains. Habitable zone world but too cold and dry for unassisted life.

planets.name: Snuffer
planets.notes: Dense, dark-surfaced body with very low albedo. Extremely rich in carbon compounds, giving it a coal-black appearance in reflected light.

planets.name: Guttering
planets.notes: Distant ice world with a methane-nitrogen atmosphere. Its four small moons are likely captured asteroids from the system's sparse outer debris field.

anomalies.name: The Dimming
anomalies.notes: Last Lantern A exhibits irregular micro-dimming events lasting hours to days. Not consistent with known starspot patterns or transiting bodies. Cause unknown.

faction_control.notes: Unclaimed. Located deep in the Rimward Barrens, far from any faction's sphere of influence.

history: Last Lantern was identified by the Rimward Barrens automated survey in 2496. Its binary nature was not confirmed until parallax measurements in 2501 revealed the distant M-dwarf companion.

The system was informally named by the survey team for its position as the last cataloged star along their outbound vector before the instruments could no longer resolve individual systems against the galactic background.

The anomalous dimming events were first noted in archival photometry data in 2547. A brief proposal to redirect a deep-space telescope for closer observation was rejected due to the system's extreme remoteness.
description: Last Lantern is a binary system in the emptiest stretch of the Rimward Barrens — two aging stars, one deep orange and one dark red, separated by 87 AU of vacuum. The primary's four planets orbit close in, huddled around a star that was never particularly bright and grows dimmer with age. Wick and Snuffer are bare rocks; Tallow is a frozen near-miss at habitability; Guttering is an ice world attended by captured debris. The companion star is visible from any of them as a dim red point, not much brighter than a planet.

The system takes its name from its position at the edge of the known. When the Rimward Barrens survey pushed outward, Last Lantern was the final star they cataloged before the stellar density dropped below their instruments' resolution threshold. Beyond it, the gaps between stars grow vast and the galaxy thins toward the intergalactic void. It is, in a navigational sense, the last light before the dark.

The irregular dimming of the primary star adds an unsettling footnote to an otherwise unremarkable system. The micro-dimming events follow no detectable pattern and match no known stellar phenomenon at this spectral class. Some astronomers have speculated about unusual circumstellar material; others suggest instrument artifacts in the aging survey data. Without a dedicated observation campaign — unlikely given the system's remoteness — the cause of Last Lantern's flickering will remain unknown.
